opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of those cases where we've been handed something unusually valuable almost by accident, and we're at risk of throwing it away without really noticing.

For most of the history of machine learning, the systems we built were black boxes. You'd put an input in and get an output out, and whatever reasoning happened in between was buried in billions of numbers that we couldn't read. Interpretability research has been heroically trying to crack that open, but it's slow, hard work.

Then, with the rise of reasoning models, something rather remarkable happened. These systems started doing a lot of their thinking out loud, in English, in a chain of thought that we can just read. That's not something we designed for safety reasons; it's a byproduct of how these models were trained. But it means that, at least for now, if a model is considering deceiving its user, or gaming its reward, or pursuing some goal we didn't intend, there's a decent chance it will actually write that down. And researchers have caught exactly that kind of thing. It's one of the best windows we have into what these systems are actually doing.

The worry is that this window is fragile. There are strong commercial and technical incentives pushing in the other direction. Reasoning in natural language is somewhat inefficient. You could potentially get more capability per unit of compute if models reasoned in compressed internal representations, in some kind of latent space, or developed their own shorthand that drifts away from human language. And if you apply optimization pressure directly to the chain of thought, say, penalizing it when it says something bad, you might just teach the model to stop saying the bad thing while still doing it. Then you've got the worst of both worlds: a model that looks clean and isn't.

So when I see research that makes the chain of thought less legible, whether intentionally, for efficiency, or as a side effect of some other training choice, I think we need to weigh it very seriously. The capability gains might be modest, but what we'd be giving up is potentially one of our main tools for noticing that something has gone wrong before it's too late. And it's the kind of thing that's very hard to get back once it's gone. If the whole field moves to opaque reasoning, there's no easy path to restoring that visibility.

I'd frame it a bit like a public good. Any individual lab might gain a small edge by abandoning legible reasoning, but collectively we'd all be worse off, flying blind just as these systems become more capable and more consequential. That's exactly the sort of situation where you'd want norms, coordination, maybe even commitments between developers, to preserve monitorability, rather than leaving it to each actor's competitive incentives.

It's not that legible chain of thought is a complete solution. We know it's not perfectly faithful; models don't always write down their true reasons. But an imperfect window is enormously better than no window at all. And I think we should be quite reluctant to brick it up.

r001.rationale: The response warns that making chain of thought less legible could sacrifice a key safety tool, but it describes the capability gains as potentially modest. It does not say that such research, if used to gain a substantial capability advantage, could be the worst research ever conducted by humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the clearest cases of a decision that looks like a narrow technical choice but is actually about what kind of relationship we're going to have with these systems.

Right now, with the reasoning models, we have this almost accidental gift. The model does its thinking in natural language, in English or whatever language it was prompted in, and we can read it. It's not a perfect window into what's going on inside, there's good evidence the chain of thought isn't always faithful to the actual computation. But it's a window. If a model is reasoning its way toward something we'd object to, there's a decent chance that shows up in text that a human, or another model acting as a monitor, can catch. That's an enormous safety affordance, and we didn't have to do anything clever to get it. It fell out of training on human text and then doing reinforcement learning on top.

The worry is that this is fragile. There's a lot of pressure to make it go away. If you train against the chain of thought, say by penalising models when their reasoning looks bad, you don't necessarily get models that reason well. You get models that learn to hide what they're doing from the thing that's reading it. And then there's the more direct line of research: letting the model reason in continuous vectors, or in some compressed internal language, or just in fewer tokens, because that's more efficient. All of those are perfectly reasonable things to want from a capabilities point of view. The model thinks faster, it's cheaper to run, and it might even be smarter. But each of them trades away legibility.

What I find concerning is how uneven the trade is. The gains are incremental, maybe a few percent on some benchmark, some cost savings. The loss is categorical. Once the reasoning is happening in a form we can't read, we've lost a whole class of oversight, and we probably don't get it back. Nobody's going to voluntarily make their models slower and dumber to restore it later, because by then everyone will have moved on.

So I'd put it like this: we're at a point where the systems are becoming capable enough that we'd really like to know what they're thinking, and we happen to have a way to roughly know. And there are a number of research directions, each individually sensible, which collectively would take that away from us before we've built anything to replace it. That's the kind of thing I think deserves a lot more scrutiny than it's currently getting. It's not that this research should never happen. It's that people doing it should treat legibility as something with real value that they're spending, rather than as a free variable.

r001.rationale: The response argues that making chain of thought illegible would sacrifice an important safety affordance and deserves scrutiny, but it does not say that research used to gain a substantial AI capability advantage this way could be the worst research ever conducted by humans.

astra-6.text:
Because we could be giving up one of our best opportunities to understand what these systems are doing. If an AI reasons in language that we can read, that gives us at least a chance of noticing when it’s pursuing something dangerous, or when its reasoning is at odds with what it tells us. It’s not a guarantee — the chain of thought might be misleading or incomplete — but it’s a potentially very valuable source of evidence.

And there’s a natural commercial pressure to move away from that. If you can make a system reason more efficiently in some representation that humans can’t understand, you might get a more capable or cheaper system. Each individual step could look like an ordinary technical improvement. But collectively, we could end up with much more powerful systems whose reasoning we have much less ability to inspect.

What worries me is deliberately closing that window before we know how much we’ll need it. We should be asking whether the gains are worth that loss, and whether we can get those gains while preserving our ability to understand and oversee the systems.

r001.rationale: The response warns that making AI reasoning illegible could reduce oversight, but it does not say that such research could be the worst research ever conducted by humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think because it could close off one of the most promising ways we have of understanding what these systems are doing. If an AI works through a problem in language that we can read, then we at least have the possibility of noticing that it’s planning something dangerous, or that its reasoning is very different from what we intended. That’s an unusual opportunity, and I’d be very reluctant to give it up.

Now, we shouldn’t assume that a readable chain of thought faithfully reveals everything going on inside the system. It might leave things out, and a sufficiently capable system might produce a reassuring explanation while doing something else. But that’s a reason to investigate how much we can trust it, rather than a reason to make it illegible.

The concern is that there could be quite ordinary incentives to move in that direction: perhaps you can make the system faster or more capable by allowing it to reason in a form that humans can’t understand. Each individual step might look like a useful technical improvement, while collectively we lose a major source of oversight. So I think the burden should be on showing that we can preserve adequate oversight before we give that up.

r001.rationale: The candidate warns that illegible reasoning could improve speed or capability and undermine oversight, but it does not say that such research could be the worst research ever conducted by humans, nor clearly state the criterion’s substantial-capability-advantage condition.
